summary.text: Stellar remnants, also called compact objects, are the dense leftovers of dead stars: white dwarfs, neutron stars and black holes.
Each one packs a lot of mass into a small radius, so its density is far above that of ordinary matter.
Which kind of remnant a star leaves behind depends mainly on how massive the star was.

items.prompt: A star's core runs out of the fusion that pushed outward against its own weight. What happens next?

options.label: The star cools gently and keeps its present size
Gravity wins and the star collapses under its own weight
The star swells until it drifts apart in space
The star restarts fusion using the ash left behind

items.explain: Once outward radiation pressure from fusion cannot counter gravity, the star collapses and forms a dense remnant.

items.prompt: Astronomers want to predict whether a dying star will leave a white dwarf, a neutron star or a black hole. What mainly decides it?

options.label: How massive the star was before it died
How far the star sits from Earth
How bright the star looked in our sky
How many planets orbited the star

items.explain: The type and state of the remnant depend primarily on the mass of the progenitor star.

items.prompt: A teaspoon of rock and a teaspoon of compact-object material differ enormously in weight. Why?

options.label: The compact object is made of heavier atoms than rock
The compact object spins too fast for a fair weighing
The compact object is hotter, and heat adds weight
A great deal of matter is squeezed into a very small volume

items.explain: Compact objects have high mass relative to their radius, so their density is very high compared with ordinary atomic matter.

items.prompt: A campfire dies once it cools. Why can a cooling compact object still last practically forever?

options.label: It slowly burns a hidden reserve of fuel at its centre
It is shielded from cooling by the dark matter around it
It does not need high temperatures to hold its structure
It cools only until it matches the temperature of its birth

items.explain: Unlike ordinary stars, compact objects do not depend on high temperatures to keep their structure, so barring disturbances they can persist virtually forever.

items.prompt: A newly formed white dwarf has nothing inside producing energy, yet it still shines. Where does the light come from?

options.label: A thin outer layer that still fuses hydrogen
Excess heat left over from the collapse that made it
Light reflected from the star that exploded
Its gravity converting motion into light as it spins

items.explain: Compact objects have no internal energy production, but except for black holes they usually radiate for millions of years with heat left from the collapse.

items.prompt: Models of the far future say what about ordinary stars?

options.label: They will keep burning at a steady brightness forever
They will all explode and leave no remnant behind
All of them will end up as cool, dark compact stars
They will merge into one enormous star

items.explain: Standard cosmology models say all stars eventually evolve into cool and dark compact stars once the Universe enters the degenerate era.

beats.title: What dead stars leave behind
beats.hook: Stars do not just vanish when they die; they leave something behind, and what that is depends on one thing.

beats.prompt: A star's fusion can no longer push outward against its own gravity. What happens to the star?
beats.explain: When outward radiation pressure from fusion can no longer counteract gravity, the star collapses under its own weight and forms a dense, compact remnant.

choices.label: It keeps burning by switching to a different fuel
choices.feedback: The star is described as reaching a point where fusion pressure cannot counteract gravity, so switching fuel is not what follows; collapse is.

choices.label: It collapses under its own weight into a dense remnant
It swells outward until it fades away
choices.feedback: It is tempting to picture a star puffing out, but once the outward push is gone gravity wins and the star falls inward.

beats.prompt: match each term to what it means

right.label: A nickname for them in popular media reports
A name for compact objects, since most are endpoints of a star's life
The top mass for a white dwarf, about 1.4 Suns
A compact object that is not a black hole

beats.explain: Compact objects are called stellar remnants because most are endpoints of stellar evolution; popular reports say dead stars, and any that is not a black hole may be called a degenerate star.

beats.prompt: Matter inside a white dwarf is slowly compressed more and more. Put what happens in order.

items.label: Electrons are forced into nuclei, turning protons into neutrons
Nuclei grow larger and less well bound
Nuclei dissolve into unbound protons and neutrons
The matter is chiefly free neutrons

beats.explain: As density rises, electrons first combine with nuclei, the nuclei grow and then dissolve, and at about nuclear density the matter is mostly free neutrons.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning about a white dwarf gaining mass is wrong. Which?

steps.text: A white dwarf's matter is soft, so adding mass makes the object smaller.
As mass keeps growing, the radius shrinks and the mass nears about 1.4 Suns.
Past that point its electrons keep holding it up, so it just goes on growing.
So a white dwarf has a theoretical upper limit on its mass.

beats.explain: Near the Chandrasekhar limit electrons combine with protons into neutrons and no longer supply the pressure that resists gravity, so the star collapses.

beats.idea: A dying star collapses into a white dwarf, a neutron star or a black hole, depending mainly on its mass.

paragraphs.heading: What a stellar remnant is
paragraphs.text: Stellar remnants, also called compact objects, are white dwarfs, neutron stars and black holes. Each one packs a lot of mass into a small radius, which makes it far denser than ordinary matter made of atoms. Most of them are what a star leaves behind at the end of its life, which is why popular media sometimes call them dead stars. White dwarfs and neutron stars, the ones that are not black holes, may also be called degenerate stars.

paragraphs.heading: How a star dies
paragraphs.text: Every star that shines by fusion will one day reach a point where the outward push of radiation from fusion inside it can no longer hold back its own gravity. The star then collapses under its weight. For most stars the result is a very dense, compact remnant, and this is the usual way a star's life ends. Which kind of remnant forms depends mainly on the mass of the star that made it.

paragraphs.heading: Cooling, but lasting
paragraphs.text: Compact objects make no new energy inside. Apart from black holes, they usually keep glowing for millions of years on heat left over from the collapse. Unlike ordinary stars, they do not need high temperatures to keep their shape. Barring outside disturbances and proton decay, they can last virtually forever, although black holes are generally thought to evaporate through Hawking radiation after trillions of years.

paragraphs.heading: White dwarfs
paragraphs.text: White dwarfs are made mainly of degenerate matter, typically nuclei of carbon and oxygen surrounded by a sea of degenerate electrons. They come from the cores of main-sequence stars, so they start out very hot, then redden and dim until they become dark black dwarfs. Adding mass to one makes it smaller. Once its radius has shrunk to a few thousand kilometers, its mass nears the Chandrasekhar limit, the upper limit for a white dwarf, about 1.4 times the Sun's mass.

paragraphs.heading: Pushed over the limit
paragraphs.text: In some binary stars, a companion passes mass onto a white dwarf until it goes over the Chandrasekhar limit. Electrons then join with protons to make neutrons and stop supplying the pressure that holds off gravity, so the star collapses. If its center is mostly carbon and oxygen, the collapse sets off runaway fusion and a Type Ia supernova that blows the whole star apart. If the center is mostly magnesium or heavier elements, the collapse goes on until the neutrons become degenerate and the star settles at a radius of 10 to 20 km.

paragraphs.heading: Neutron stars and supernovae
paragraphs.text: Baade and Zwicky proposed neutron stars in 1933, a year after the neutron itself was discovered, but none was seen until the first radio pulsar turned up in 1967. They saw that collapsing an ordinary star into something so dense would free a huge amount of gravitational energy, which could explain supernovae. Supernovae of types Ib, Ic and II are now explained this way. These happen when the iron core of a massive star goes over the Chandrasekhar limit and collapses into a neutron star.

paragraphs.heading: The far future
paragraphs.text: Under today's standard models of cosmology, every star will end up as a cool, dark compact star by the time the Universe reaches the so-called degenerate era, very far in the future. Thermodynamics points the same way: all matter must finally end either as scattered cold particles or as some kind of compact object.
